decisions.quote:
Numerous developmental studies of predominantly urban Western middle-class children suggest
that children reach this milestone by 18 to 24 months of age. By 18 months, approximately 50%
pass and by 24 months a significant majority of children (more than 70%) are reported to self-
refer by touching or removing a mark from their own body (face or other body region) while
exploring their mirror image (Amsterdam, 1972; Asendorpf, Warkentin, & Baudonnière, 1996;
Bard, Todd, Bernier, Love, & Leavens, 2006; Bertenthal & Fisher, 1978; Lewis & Brooks-Gunn,
1979; Lewis & Ramsay, 2004; Nielsen, Dissanayake, & Kashima, 2003; Schulman & Kaplowitz,
1976). Here we report cross-cultural observations on the emergence of mirror self-recognition
(MSR), using a simplified mark test, raising questions regarding the meaning and universal
validity of this test as an ontogenetic benchmark of self-concept.
decisions.location: Introduction, p. 2; cf. Method (Dependent Measure, Analysis, and Reliability, p. 4), Experiment 1 Results and Discussion (p. 5), General Discussion (pp. 8-9), and References (p. 12)
decisions.reason: Addressing the unresolved scope objection: citation location or frequency alone cannot establish background status, nor can inclusion in an introductory citation cluster automatically establish a retested target. On p. 2, Broesch et al. (2010) cite Schulman and Kaplowitz (1976, "Mirror-image response during the first two years of life", Developmental Psychobiology, 10, 133-142) solely inside an eight-study omnibus parenthetical supporting the summary statement that by 18 months ~50% of Western children pass and by 24 months >70% self-refer by touching or removing a mark on their body. Primary sources supplied for sibling targets in that same eight-study cluster (asendorpf1996.txt for target_index 1, bard2006.txt for target_index 2, and nielsen2003.txt for target_index 6) demonstrate that this cluster pools heterogeneous works—for example, Asendorpf et al. (1996) tested synchronic imitation only at 18 months and Bard et al. (2006) tested procedural/scaffolding variations—rather than eight uniform benchmark reports. Conversely, for the retained benchmark studies, Broesch et al. (2010) explicitly state the specific empirical findings tested by their 18-to-72-month cross-cultural mark-test experiments: Amsterdam (1972; shipped input_row_index 843), Bertenthal and Fisher (1978; target_index 3), and Lewis and Brooks-Gunn (1979; target_index 4) are explicitly identified as reporting that >60% (60% to 85%) of Western middle-class children older than 20 months pass the mark test, which directly defines the .60 probability threshold tested in the one-tailed binomial analyses of Experiments 1 and 2 (Method, p. 4; General Discussion, p. 8), and Lewis and Ramsay (2004; target_index 5) is explicitly identified as reporting >80% passing by 21 months and 100% by 24 months using a comparable spontaneous mark-test procedure (Results, p. 5; General Discussion, p. 9). Unlike those retained studies, Broesch et al. (2010) never state an individual empirical finding from Schulman and Kaplowitz (1976), and unlike targets 1, 2, and 6, no primary text or abstract of Schulman and Kaplowitz (1976) is present in the supplied evidence. The precise unresolved question is whether Schulman and Kaplowitz (1976) itself reported the specific 18-to-24-month mark-directed self-recognition pass-rate finding retested in Experiments 1 and 2 or was cited only for general developmental background on infant mirror-image responses.

decisions.quote:
In Roter’s study, as well as in ours, the
quality of technical-medical care (‘‘profi-
ciency”) was better explained by RIAS task-
clusters than by RIAS socio-emotional clus-
ters. Also, in Roter’s study, as well as in ours,
“giving information” and, especially, “giv-
ing medical information” proved to be im-
portant in the assessed quality of care.
decisions.location: Discussion, p. 293 (also Abstract, p. 283; Introduction, p. 284; Methods, pp. 285-287; References 7-8, p. 296)
decisions.reason: Addressing the unresolved objection using the replicating text and both supplied primary abstracts (3695653.txt and 3695654.txt): Hall, Roter, and Katz (1987, "Task versus socio-emotional behaviors in physicians", Med Care 1987;25:399-412; Reference 7, represented in shipped row input_row_index 649, DOI 10.1097/00005650-198705000-00004) and Roter, Hall, and Katz (1987, "Relations between physicians’ behaviors and analogue patients’ satisfaction, recall and impressions", Med Care 1987;25:437; Reference 8, candidate target_index 1) are two companion articles from the same analogue-patient study of 43 primary care physicians interacting with two standardized simulated-patient cases, scored with RIAS, speech error counts, and filtered-audio vocal affect ratings. As the primary abstracts establish, Reference 7 (3695653.txt, shipped row 649) scored the encounter transcripts for "physician proficiency" and analyzed the internal associations among physicians' task-oriented, verbal socioemotional, and vocal-affect behaviors and their relation to physician proficiency (technical-medical quality). Reference 8 (3695654.txt) instead added ratings from 258 role-playing analogue patients to test associations between physicians' behaviors and analogue patients' satisfaction, recall of information, and global impressions. In Bensing and Dronkers (1992), "only general practitioner (GP) behavior is studied. GP’s behavior is related to panel-assessed quality of care on three separate dimensions (technical-medical, psychosocial, and the management of the physician-patient relationship)" (Abstract, p. 283). Bensing and Dronkers collect no patient satisfaction, patient recall, or patient impression data and do not retest the analogue-patient satisfaction/recall/impression findings unique to Reference 8. Instead, they treat References 7 and 8 jointly as a single study ("Roter’s study", "Hall and Roter’s study", "a study into the relative contribution of affective and instrumental behavior to the quality of care ('medical proficiency').7,8", p. 284), empirically retest the internal correlations among RIAS task, verbal socioemotional, and nonverbal affect measures (Tables 2-3) and their associations with panel-assessed quality of care/"proficiency" (Tables 4-5; Discussion, p. 293), and quote Reference 8 for the concluding call at the end of the two-paper sequence to replicate the study in a natural setting using video (p. 293). Because the underlying study and the specific empirical findings actually retested by Bensing and Dronkers are already represented by shipped row input_row_index 649 (Reference 7), Reference 8 is not a genuinely missing original target.

corrected_value.title: The effects of torture: Two community studies

decisions.quote: Partial correlation and hierarchical regression results found that torture trauma and torture severity were not significant predictors of PTSD, other cumulative life traumas that happened before and after torture were the highly significant predictors. These results replicated previous findings of Kira et al., 2006;and Hollifield et al., 2011.
decisions.location: Discussion (also Introduction; Methods - Hypotheses; Results - Partial Correlation Results and Hierarchical Multiple Regression Analyses Results, Table 2.2; References)
decisions.reason: The paper explicitly attributes to Kira et al. (2006, Peace and Conflict: Journal of Peace Psychology, 12(3), 205-228, DOI 10.1207/s15327949pac1203_1) the specific empirical finding from two community studies of Iraqi refugees that torture did not predict elevated PTSD symptoms after controlling for cumulative traumas occurring before and after torture (Introduction). It directly retests this finding in a new clinical sample of 326 refugee torture survivors from 30 countries using the Cumulative Trauma Scale (CTS) in Hypothesis 1, partial correlations, and step-three hierarchical multiple regression (Table 2.2), and explicitly states in the Discussion that the results replicated the previous findings of both Kira et al. (2006) and Hollifield et al. (2011). The sole shipped original (input_row_index 2503, Hollifield, Warner, & Westermeyer, 2011, Journal of Nervous & Mental Disease, 199(1), 3-10, DOI 10.1097/nmd.0b013e3182051501) and sibling targets 2 (Başoğlu, 2009), 3 (Hooberman et al., 2007), and 4 (Punamäki et al., 2010) are independent studies by different author teams in different years and journals, so report equivalence does not apply.

corrected_value.title: A multivariate contextual analysis of torture and cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatments: Implications for an evidence-based definition of torture

decisions.quote: For torture types, while physical torture did not predict PTSD or CTD, witnessing or psychological torture predicted CTD, and PTSD, replicating Basoglu et al.'s (2009) findings.
decisions.location: Discussion (also Introduction; Methods - Torture severity scale; Results - Partial Correlation Results, Table 1.1; References)
decisions.reason: The paper explicitly attributes to Başoğlu (2009, American Journal of Orthopsychiatry, 79(2), 135-145, DOI 10.1037/a0015681) the empirical finding that psychological torture rather than physical torture predicts PTSD (Introduction). It empirically retests the differential associations of physical torture versus witnessing/psychological torture subscales with PTSD and CTD in a new clinical sample of 326 refugee torture survivors (Results, Table 1.1: witnessing/psychological torture correlates r = .15* with PTSD and r = .13* with CTD, whereas physical torture correlates r = .06 with PTSD and r = -.003 with CTD) and explicitly concludes in the Discussion that these results replicated Başoğlu's (2009) findings. This original work is completely distinct from shipped row input_row_index 2503 (Hollifield, Warner, & Westermeyer, 2011, DOI 10.1097/nmd.0b013e3182051501) and from sibling targets 0 (Kira et al., 2006), 3 (Hooberman et al., 2007), and 4 (Punamäki et al., 2010), so report equivalence does not apply.
